guides.title: Hash maps: pairs and frequencies
guides.summary: Use a map to remember exactly what the current step needs from the past.

sections.title: Unsorted two-sum and distinct indices
paragraphs: A quadratic baseline tries every pair. A one-pass map instead asks, “Have I already seen target minus this value?” Store value → earliest index. Before index i is processed, the map contains only indices less than i. That invariant prevents reusing the same position and makes a found pair valid immediately.

For [3,3] and target 6, the first 3 has no match and is stored at index 0. The second 3 finds index 0 and returns (0,1). For [3] and target 6, there is no pair. Checking after inserting would incorrectly match the first element to itself. Use long for subtraction even when both inputs are int: target - value can exceed the int range.

Expected time is O(n) with hashing and extra space O(n); adversarial collisions can worsen lookup cost. Sorting plus two pointers uses a different tradeoff and loses original indices unless you retain them. Clarify whether the task wants a pair, all pairs, unique values, or a count: those need different duplicate handling.
sections.example: [8, -2, 5, 7], target 3: before 5 arrives, -2 is in the map, so return indices (1,2).

sections.title: Anagrams are equality of multisets
paragraphs: An anagram has the same frequency of every symbol, not merely the same set of symbols. Count the first string, subtract the second, and reject missing/exhausted counts. A length check rejects many cases early. For a declared lowercase ASCII alphabet, an int[26] is compact; a dictionary handles the wider char domain.

The supplied method compares UTF-16 code units ordinally: case and spaces matter. A product requirement involving human characters may require Unicode normalization and Rune or grapheme iteration instead. Sorting is also a correct O(n log n) solution and can be simpler for some constraints; frequency counting is typically O(n) expected time, O(alphabet) space. For anagram substrings, maintain frequencies in a fixed-size window rather than recounting every substring.
sections.example: “aab” and “abb” contain the same distinct letters but are not anagrams: the multiplicities differ.

guides.title: Two pointers and in-place compaction
guides.summary: Eliminate candidates with a reason, or separate the read and write positions.

sections.title: Sorted pair sum
paragraphs: Start at both ends of an ascending array. If the sum is too small, even the largest available partner cannot rescue the current left value, so discard that left position. If it is too large, even the smallest available partner cannot rescue the current right value, so discard that right position. This elimination argument is the reason the algorithm works; “two pointers” is only its shape.

The invariant is that any remaining valid pair lies between the pointers. Stop while left < right so a position cannot match itself. Each step removes one position, giving O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Widen one addend to long before adding to avoid overflow. On unsorted input these eliminations are invalid: use hashing or sort a copy, retaining original indices if required.
sections.example: [1,4,6,9], target 10: endpoints already match. Target 11: 1+9 is too small, then 4+9 too large, then 4+6 too small: absent.

sections.title: Palindromes and reversal
paragraphs: A strict palindrome compares corresponding ends; the processed outer region is already known to mirror. A reversal swaps those ends; the processed outer region is already in its final position. Both move inward, using O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. Strings are immutable in C#, so reverse a char[] if mutation is needed.

Clarify normalization before coding: exact ordinal comparison, ignoring punctuation, case-insensitive comparison, and Unicode grapheme comparison are different contracts. The sample deliberately implements exact UTF-16 comparison. Empty and singleton strings are palindromes; an odd-length center needs no comparison.

sections.title: O(1) space is a constraint, not a pattern
paragraphs: For compaction, maintain [0,write) as the retained prefix and let read scan every original position. Copy a retained value to write and increment write. Because write never exceeds read, unread values are not overwritten. Return the logical prefix length; the unused suffix is unspecified.

Index marking and cyclic placement require much stronger assumptions: values must map into valid indices and mutation must be permitted. Negation markers need positive values, special handling for zero, and care with int.MinValue. Do not pick them solely because the prompt says O(1). Output storage and recursion stack usually count separately from auxiliary space, so state exactly what you are excluding.
sections.example: [0,7,0,4] compacts to a meaningful prefix [7,4], length 2; the suffix is not part of the result.

guides.title: Sliding windows: fixed, longest, and shortest
guides.summary: A window works only when moving a boundary preserves a useful monotone relationship.

sections.title: Exactly k contiguous items
paragraphs: Keep the aggregate of the current k-item window. Add the new right value, remove the value that just fell out at right-k, and update the answer only once k values exist. A sum can be updated in O(1); a maximum cannot simply subtract the outgoing maximum and may need a monotonic deque.

Use long for accumulated sums, and initialize a maximum to a real first window or long.MinValue so all-negative inputs work. Reject k <= 0 and k > n unless the problem defines another behavior. Negative numbers do not invalidate fixed-size sums: both boundaries are controlled by size. O(n) time, O(1) extra space for the sum version.
sections.example: [4,-2,3,1], k=2 gives sums 2,1,4; the answer is 4.

sections.title: Longest valid window and at most k distinct
paragraphs: For at-most-k distinct characters, adding a character can make a valid window invalid; deleting from the left cannot introduce a new distinct character. Keep a frequency map for exactly the current window, shrink while distinct count exceeds k, then measure the restored valid window. Remove zero-count keys or Count stops meaning “distinct characters present.”

At the measurement point the entire [left,right] window is valid, and left never moves backwards. Each position enters and leaves once, so the nested while loop still costs O(n) expected time. k=0 correctly produces length zero. The supplied code counts UTF-16 code units and returns a length, not a substring.

“Longest/shortest substring” alone is not enough to choose this technique. You need an efficiently maintainable condition and a reason discarded boundaries will not become useful later. Arbitrary sum constraints with negative numbers often break that reasoning.
sections.example: “eceba”, k=2: “ece” has length 3. Adding b forces removal of both leading e and c before the window has only two distinct symbols.

sections.title: Shortest valid uses a different loop
paragraphs: For strictly positive values and target sum, expansion increases the sum and shrinking decreases it. Expand right; while sum is already large enough, record the candidate and shrink to try a shorter one. This is the opposite measurement order from longest-at-most-k: measure before removing the value that may make the window invalid.

The positive-value contract is essential. With negatives, a large sum may become smaller after expansion, and deleting a negative can increase it. Prefix sums, a map, or a monotonic deque may be needed instead. A single if shrink is also valid in some specialized algorithms; use while when your proof requires restoring validity each iteration.
sections.example: [2,1,4,2], target 6: [2,1,4] works, shrinking finds [4,2] of length 2.

guides.title: Prefix sums: differences and subarray counts
guides.summary: Replace repeated range work with cumulative state.

sections.title: Count subarrays summing to k
paragraphs: Let P[j] be the sum before position j. A subarray [i,j) sums to P[j]-P[i]. For a target k, each earlier prefix equal to P[j]-k creates one valid subarray ending at j-1. Store a frequency, not a boolean: several earlier prefixes can have the same sum.

Seed frequency[0]=1 for the empty prefix so a subarray starting at index zero is countable. Query the required earlier prefix before adding the current prefix; otherwise k=0 can count an empty subarray at the current boundary. Negative values and zeros work without special cases because the proof uses algebra rather than monotonicity.

Expected time is O(n), memory O(n). Both running sums and answer counts need long: an all-zero array has n(n+1)/2 nonempty subarrays. A boolean set or storing only one index loses counts. To find the longest target-sum subarray instead, store each prefix’s earliest index.
sections.example: [1,-1,1], k=1: at successive steps the contributions are 1,0,2, total 3.

sections.title: Reusable half-open range sums
paragraphs: Build n+1 prefixes with prefix[0]=0 and prefix[i+1]=prefix[i]+values[i]. Then sum over [left,right) is prefix[right]-prefix[left]. Half-open endpoints make empty ranges and ranges starting at zero natural. Build in O(n), answer each immutable query in O(1), use O(n) extra space.

Updates invalidate later prefixes. For an interview focused on static range queries, do not jump to a Fenwick or segment tree. Explain that many interleaved updates and queries would change the required structure. Always state whether right is inclusive; most off-by-one failures come from mixing conventions.

guides.title: Linked lists: identity, rewiring, and sentinels
guides.summary: Save links before overwriting them, and reason about node identity.

sections.title: Cycle detection and the middle
paragraphs: A slow pointer moves one link while fast moves two. In an acyclic list fast reaches null. In a cycle their relative position advances one step per iteration, so they eventually meet. Compare node references, not values; equal values in different nodes do not imply a cycle. The empty list must return false, so check for a meeting only after advancing.

For the middle of an acyclic list, the same speed relationship means slow has covered half the links when fast reaches the end. The supplied loop returns the second middle for an even length. A cycle-detection method returning bool does not also return the middle; use the separate Middle method. Both run O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
sections.example: 1→2→3→4 returns node 3 as the second middle. If node 4 points to node 2, HasCycle returns true.

sections.title: Reverse a list or bounded range
paragraphs: Before each full-reversal iteration, previous is the reversed processed prefix and current starts the untouched suffix. Save next first, point current.Next backward, then advance both variables. If you overwrite Next before saving it, you lose the remaining list. The resulting head is previous, including null for empty input.

For a subrange, a dummy node anchors the position before the range even when the head changes. Repeatedly take the node after the range’s tail and move it to the front of the range. The example validates 1-based inclusive bounds before mutation. Clarify whether callers expect the original list preserved; these methods intentionally reuse and mutate nodes. O(n) time, O(1) extra space.

sections.title: Merge and dummy-node reasoning
paragraphs: A dummy node gives every appended node a predecessor, removing the special case for the first real node. Tail marks the merged result’s last node. Repeatedly attach the smaller current head, advance only that source, then advance tail. Once one list ends, attach the other suffix unchanged.

The invariant is a sorted completed prefix and two still-sorted remaining suffixes. Choosing from a on equality makes the merge stable across the two sources. Inputs must be acyclic and disjoint when nodes are reused: shared tails can create accidental cycles. Time O(m+n), auxiliary space O(1). Sentinels are also useful for deletion or insertion before the current head, but not mandatory when a simple explicit head case is clearer.

guides.title: Stacks, from the beginning
guides.summary: Learn what a stack remembers, how to use it in C#, and why it fits nested brackets. Next-greater problems are an optional second lesson.

sections.title: Start here: what is a stack?
paragraphs: A stack is a collection of items with one rule about how you use it: add an item at one end, and remove the most recently added item from that same end. Think of a pile of plates. You put a new plate on top, and the next plate you take is the one on top. The plate underneath becomes available after you remove it.

That accessible end is called the top. It is not the largest value, and it is not a special kind of item. It is simply the position of the most recent item that has not yet been removed. If you add 10 and then 20, the top holds 20. Removing 20 exposes 10.

This order is called last in, first out, usually shortened to LIFO. A stack does not sort its contents. If you add 20 and then 10, you remove 10 first because it arrived last, even though it is smaller.

This guide assumes you can read a C# loop, but it does not assume you have used a stack. Read through “Check the basics” first. The later next-greater sections introduce a separate, more advanced use of the same collection; you can leave them for another session.

sections.title: Using Push, Pop, Peek, and Count in C#
paragraphs: C# provides Stack<T> in System.Collections.Generic. The T is the type of item you want to store, so Stack<int> stores integers and Stack<char> stores characters. Creating a stack gives you an empty collection.

Push(x) adds x at the top. Pop() removes the top item and returns it, so you can use the value you removed. Peek() returns the top item without removing it. Count is a property that tells you how many items remain; it has no parentheses.

Follow the state before reading the code. After Push(10), the stack contains [10]. After Push(20), it contains [10, 20], with 20 at the top. Peek() returns 20 and leaves both items in place. Pop() then returns 20 and leaves [10]. Another Pop() returns 10 and leaves an empty stack. Throughout this guide, items in square brackets are written from bottom to top, so the rightmost item is the top.

Pop() and Peek() throw InvalidOperationException on an empty stack: there is no item to return. Check Count > 0 before calling them when emptiness is possible. TryPop(out item) is another option: it removes an item and returns true on success, or returns false on an empty stack. Only use item when it succeeds. TryPeek works the same way without removing anything. The complete example below can be called as StackBasics.Demonstrate() from a console program.

sections.title: Why use a stack instead of an array or a list?
paragraphs: An array or List<T> lets you access an item by its position, such as items[3]. You could use the end of a list as a stack by adding and removing only there. Stack<T> gives that rule a name and an API: your code asks for the latest item rather than choosing an arbitrary position. Its normal operations do not let you reach into the middle by index.

The restriction is useful when the newest unfinished thing must be handled first. For example, imagine an editor recording “type A” and then “type B.” Undo should reverse “type B” before “type A.” A stack could hold the information needed to reverse each action. The stack only supplies the order; your program must still implement what undoing an action means.

Nested brackets have the same order: an inner pair must close before the outer pair. That is the example we will work through next. By contrast, a waiting line serves the earliest arrival first, so it usually needs a queue. If you need frequent access to arbitrary positions, an array or list is usually clearer.
A useful question is “What does one stored item mean, and why is the most recent one the next one I need?” Being able to answer that is more useful than matching a problem title to a data structure.

sections.title: Worked example: why brackets need the most recent opener
paragraphs: We want to write a method that returns true when a string of brackets is properly paired and nested. It accepts the characters (, ), [, ], {, and }. Every opening bracket must have a later closing bracket of the same type, and an inner pair must finish before the pair around it. Under this contract, empty input is valid, while any non-bracket character is invalid.

For example, “([])” is valid: the square-bracket pair is inside the parentheses. “([)]” is invalid even though it has one of each opener and closer. When ) arrives, the [ is still open. We cannot close the outer parentheses through an unfinished inner pair, so merely counting brackets is not enough.

We will use a stack to remember opening brackets that have not yet been matched. The top is the most recently seen unmatched opener. When a closing bracket arrives, that top item is the only opener it is allowed to match. Here is the complete walk through “([])”. The square brackets around each state describe the collection; the quoted characters are the items inside it.
bullets: Before reading anything, the stack is empty: []. There are no unmatched opening brackets yet.
Read “(”. It starts a new pair, so push it. The stack is now ["("], and “(” is the top.
Read “[”. It starts an inner pair, so push it above “(”. The stack is now ["(", "["], and “[” is the top.
Read “]”. It must match “[”. Pop the top opener, check that it is “[”, and continue. The stack is now ["("].
Read “)”. It must match “(”. Pop and check the top again. The stack becomes [].
The string has ended and no opener remains, so return true.
sections.example: If the input were “([)]”, the third character would be “)”, but the top would still be “[”. That mismatch is enough to return false immediately. We must not search deeper for a “(” and skip the “[”.

sections.title: Turn the bracket walkthrough into code
paragraphs: The loop below makes the same decision for each character. An opener is pushed and left waiting. For a closer, the switch chooses the opener we expect. We then check for an empty stack before calling Pop(), and compare the removed opener with that expected character.

An empty stack at a closer means there is nothing to match, as in “]”. A mismatch means the nesting is wrong, as in “([)]”. Finally, a nonempty stack after the loop means an opener never closed, as in “(()”. This last check is essential even if every closer we encountered matched.

Call StackBrackets.IsBalanced("([])") to get true, or StackBrackets.IsBalanced("([)]") to get false. This is a complete C# source file; the class groups the method so it can be called from the example test program.

sections.title: Check the basics before moving on
paragraphs: The bracket method works because the stack always contains exactly the openers we have seen but have not matched, in the order we saw them. That is the fact we keep true throughout the loop. You may hear this kind of always-true fact called an invariant. Here, it explains why looking only at the top is sufficient.

For n input characters, we visit each character once and each opener is pushed and popped at most once. The total work therefore grows in proportion to the input length: O(n) time. If the input is all openers, we store n of them at once, so the worst-case extra space is O(n).

For the collection itself, Peek, Pop, and Count take constant time, O(1): they do not scan the stack. A Push is usually O(1), but C# occasionally needs to grow its internal storage and copy existing items. Across a long sequence of pushes, the average work per push is still O(1). That is what “amortized O(1)” means here.
Before going further, close the guide and explain these aloud. If one feels unclear, revisit that part; you do not need the advanced section to understand or practice ordinary stacks.
bullets: If you push 4, then 9, then call Peek twice, what does each call return, and how many items remain? What changes if the second call is Pop?
Why does “([)]” fail even though the counts of opening and closing brackets agree?
What must be true before calling Pop(), and why must the bracket method also check the stack after the loop?

sections.title: Optional next lesson: values waiting for a larger value
paragraphs: This is a new problem, not another rule you must memorize about every stack. Continue when Push, Pop, and Peek feel familiar. We will still store unfinished work, but now a stored item means “this position has not found its answer yet.”

For each number in an array, find the first strictly larger number to its right. “First” means closest in position, not largest in value. For [4, 2, 3, 5], the answer is [5, 3, 5, -1]. The 4 waits until 5; the 2 finds 3; the 3 finds 5; and the final 5 has nothing to its right. In this example, -1 is the chosen marker for no answer.

A straightforward solution starts at each position and scans right until it finds a larger number. That is a useful starting point. But in a decreasing array such as [5, 4, 3, 2], it keeps rereading the same later positions, for about n squared work overall: O(n²) time.

Instead, read the array once from left to right and remember earlier positions that are still waiting. When a new value arrives, it may be the answer for several of them. Store their indices, meaning their positions in the array, rather than only their values. An index lets us both look up the waiting value and write an answer into the correct output position. Two equal values at different positions still need separate answers.

sections.title: Walk through the waiting stack
paragraphs: For [4, 2, 3, 5], the indices are 0, 1, 2, and 3. Begin with answer = [-1, -1, -1, -1] and an empty stack. In the walkthrough, “index 0 (value 4)” explains an item; the actual stack stores only the integer index 0.

For each new value, compare it with the value at the index on top. If the new value is strictly greater, that waiting position has found its answer: pop its index and fill its answer slot. Keep doing this while the top can be answered. Then push the current index, because the current position still needs a later, greater value of its own.
bullets: At index 0, the current value is 4. Nobody is waiting, so push index 0. The waiting stack is [0], representing values [4]. The answers are still [-1, -1, -1, -1].
At index 1, the current value is 2. It cannot answer the 4 on top, because 2 is not greater than 4. Push index 1. The stack is [0, 1], representing values [4, 2].

At index 2, the current value is 3. It answers the 2 at index 1, so pop index 1 and set answer[1] = 3. The new top is index 0, whose value is 4; 3 cannot answer that one. Push index 2. The stack is now [0, 2], representing values [4, 3], and the answers are [-1, 3, -1, -1].

At index 3, the current value is 5. It first answers the 3 at index 2, then the 4 at index 0. Pop both indices and fill both answer slots. Now push index 3. The stack is [3], and the answers are [5, 3, 5, -1].
The input has ended. Index 3 is still waiting because no greater value appeared after it, so its answer stays -1.
sections.example: Notice why the inner operation is a while loop, rather than an if: the single value 5 resolved two earlier positions. Notice also that a position leaves the stack as soon as its answer is found; we never need to answer it again.

sections.title: C# for next-greater values
paragraphs: This method implements the walkthrough and returns values, not indices or distances. For example, StackNextGreater.Values(new[] { 4, 2, 3, 5 }) returns [5, 3, 5, -1]. It does not change the input array. Empty input returns an empty array; null input throws ArgumentNullException.

There are two different uses of an index in the while condition. waitingIndices.Peek() reads the most recent waiting index without removing it. values[thatIndex] then reads the number at that position. The Count check comes first, and C# short-circuits &&, so Peek is not called when the stack is empty. Only after the comparison succeeds do we Pop the index and write its answer.

The linked recall card uses a compact version of this same loop. Here, separate names for currentValue and waitingIndex make each step visible. The -1 marker follows that card’s convention; if negative inputs can make -1 a real answer, use a nullable result such as int?[] with null for absence, or return next indices instead. For example, [-2, -1] has a genuine answer of -1 at its first position.

sections.title: Why the top is enough, and why the loop is linear
paragraphs: Look at the waiting values after each step: [4], then [4, 2], then [4, 3], then [5]. From bottom to top, they never increase. This happens because we remove every smaller value from the top before adding the new value. Equal values remain: a 3 is not strictly greater than another 3.

That order explains why we can stop at the first top value that is at least as large as the current value. Every waiting value below it is at least that large too, so the current value cannot answer any of them. Conversely, every position we pop gets its first greater value: we scan left to right, and an earlier greater value would already have removed it.

A stack deliberately kept in one numeric order is called a monotonic stack. In this particular algorithm, the values at the stored indices are nonincreasing from bottom to top, meaning each next value is less than or equal to the one before it. The input array itself does not have to be sorted. The useful clue is that a new item can settle earlier unanswered questions and remove them from consideration; “the input increases” by itself is not a reason to use a stack.

The nested loops do not repeat a full scan for every position. Each index is pushed once and can be popped only once, so there are at most n pushes and n pops across the entire method. Together with at most one final unsuccessful comparison per outer step, that is O(n) total time. Up to n indices may wait at once, so extra space is O(n).

If a related problem asks how many days until a warmer temperature, the output changes: you would write i - waitingIndex, the distance between the two positions, rather than the temperature itself. First make sure you can explain this value-returning version; a related problem still needs its own definition of what is waiting and what answer to record.

sections.title: Check your understanding of the optional lesson
paragraphs: Try these with a pencil before writing another implementation. Say what every stored integer means, and show both the waiting stack and the output array after each input value. The aim is to explain the decisions, rather than recall the word “monotonic.”
bullets: For [2, 2, 3], when does each 2 receive its answer? Why does the second 2 not remove the first one?
If the stack stores index 1 and values[1] is 8, what does Peek return: 1 or 8? How would you get the other number?
Why can one current value pop several indices without making the whole algorithm O(n²)?
Before adapting the loop, state whether the required answer is a value, an index, or a distance, and what should represent no answer.

sections.title: Histogram: finish a bar when a smaller bar arrives
paragraphs: A rectangle whose limiting height is a particular bar can extend until a shorter bar blocks either side. Maintain increasing heights by index. When the current bar is shorter, pop a height: the current index is its first shorter right boundary, and the new stack top is the previous shorter-or-equal boundary under this tie convention. Width is right-left-1.

A virtual zero-height bar flushes unfinished positive bars at the end; it is not read from the array. Equal bars remain on the stack in this implementation, and one of them will eventually receive the widest valid span. Empty and zero-only histograms return zero. Nonnegative heights are required. O(n) time, O(n) stack space; multiply after widening to long.
sections.example: [2,1,2] has best area 3: height 1 across all three bars, rather than height 2 over one bar.

sections.title: Rain water: resolve the side with the lower known wall
paragraphs: Water at a position is limited by the smaller of the highest left wall and highest right wall. With two pointers, when leftMax <= rightMax, the left side already has a sufficient right barrier, so its contribution can be finalized using leftMax. Otherwise finalize the right side. Update that side’s maximum before subtracting its height.

The sample runs O(n) time and O(1) space and requires nonnegative heights. This is not the same problem as maximizing one container’s area: rain water adds many local contributions. Learn the basic monotonic stack and two-pointer proofs first; treat histogram and rainwater as optional follow-ons rather than a starting diagnostic.
sections.example: [3,0,2,0,4] traps 3+1+3=7 units over the three interior positions.

guides.title: Heaps: top-k and merging sorted streams
guides.summary: The root is the next item to remove, so choose the ordering around that operation.

sections.title: Keep the k largest by evicting the smallest
paragraphs: Maintain a min-heap containing the k largest values seen so far. Insert each value and, if size exceeds k, remove the smallest. Once all values are processed, the root is the smallest retained value, which is the kth largest overall. Duplicates count as separate positions unless the problem asks for distinct values.

For the k smallest, reverse the ordering and evict the largest instead. For k most frequent, first count values, then use frequency as the heap priority. The payload and priority need not be the same type. Validate 1<=k<=n for kth-largest; the top-frequency method allows k=0 and rejects k beyond distinct count.

Time O(n log k), auxiliary space O(k), or O(n) additional map space for frequencies. Sorting is a simpler O(n log n) baseline. Quickselect has expected O(n) time but requires partitioning, mutation decisions, and attention to worst-case behavior; it is not a prerequisite for this curriculum.
sections.example: [4,1,9,7], k=2: heap contents evolve {4}, {1,4}, {4,9}, {7,9}; root 7 is the second largest.

sections.title: Merge k sorted arrays or lists
paragraphs: Place one current head from every nonempty sorted source into a min-heap. The smallest head is the smallest remaining item globally. Emit it and replace it only with the next item from that same source. The heap therefore contains at most k candidates regardless of total output size.

The source/index payload in the sample tells you where to fetch the successor. For linked lists, the payload is the node and its successor is node.Next; decide whether to reuse nodes or allocate output. Empty sources are harmless. O(N log k) time and O(k) heap space, plus O(N) output if materializing an array. Equal priorities need no stable ordering for a value-only merge; add a tie-breaker if identity order matters.

guides.title: A running median with two heaps
guides.summary: Keep the lower and upper halves balanced and ordered.

sections.title: The two invariants
paragraphs: A max-heap holds the lower half, exposing its largest value; a min-heap holds the upper half, exposing its smallest. Maintain every lower value <= every upper value. Also keep lower.Count equal to upper.Count or exactly one larger. These two invariants make the median available from the roots alone.

Insert relative to the lower root, then move one root across if a size invariant breaks. A move preserves ordering because it transfers the boundary value. For an odd total the lower root is the median; for an even total average both roots. Widen to long before adding the int roots, then divide by 2.0 so extremes and half-integers work.

The code uses a reverse comparer for the max-heap rather than negating priorities: -int.MinValue overflows int. Add is O(log n), Median O(1), retained space O(n). Calling Median on an empty stream throws. Heaps do not automatically support efficient arbitrary removal, so a sliding-window median needs more machinery and is deliberately outside the first pass.
sections.example: Add 5,1,8,2: after rebalancing, lower contains 1,2 and upper 5,8; median is (2+5)/2=3.5.

guides.title: Binary search: exact values and boundaries
guides.summary: State the interval and prove every update removes candidates.

sections.title: Exact search on an inclusive interval
paragraphs: For exact search, [lo,hi] contains every possible remaining match. Compare the midpoint, return on equality, otherwise discard midpoint and the impossible half with lo=mid+1 or hi=mid-1. Stop when lo>hi. Empty input starts with hi=-1 and returns -1 without an access.

Use indices in the nonnegative array range, making lo+(hi-lo)/2 safe here. This expression is not universally overflow-safe for arbitrary signed numeric bounds because hi-lo itself can overflow. Exact search returns any matching duplicate. It does not promise the first occurrence. O(log n) comparisons and O(1) extra space.

sections.title: First true and lower bound
paragraphs: A first-true search assumes the predicate is false, false, …, true, true across [0,n). Keep a half-open candidate interval [lo,hi), with n also representing “no true index.” If mid is true, retain it by setting hi=mid; otherwise set lo=mid+1. The interval strictly shrinks and the predicate is never called at n.

Lower bound is the first index whose value is >= target. It can equal Length. Upper bound changes the predicate to value>target; their difference counts duplicates. Before dereferencing a lower bound, check it is inside the array and equals your target if you need an exact match.
sections.example: For [2,2,5], lower bound of 2 is 0, of 3 is 2, and of 9 is 3 (past the end).

sections.title: Rotated search needs a distinctness contract
paragraphs: With distinct values, at least one half of a rotated sorted array is ordered. Identify that half from its endpoints, test whether target belongs inside its range, and discard the other half. Preserve inclusive/exclusive comparisons around the midpoint carefully.

Duplicates such as [1,0,1,1,1] can make the ordered-half test ambiguous. A duplicate-aware version may need to shrink equal endpoints and can degrade to O(n). State the distinct-value assumption before claiming logarithmic time. Test empty, singleton, unrotated, and pivot-adjacent cases.

sections.title: Avoiding infinite loops
paragraphs: Keep each template’s loop condition and updates together. In an inclusive exact search, hi=mid can leave a one-element interval unchanged; use hi=mid-1. In a half-open boundary search, hi=mid is correct because lo<hi and mid<hi. A useful mental assertion is that interval width must decrease on every non-returning iteration.

Binary search requires ordering or a monotone predicate, not just a large input. Write the invariant before writing code, then trace arrays of length 0,1,2 and an answer outside either boundary. These tiny examples expose most interval mistakes.

guides.title: Binary search on an answer
guides.summary: Search a monotone decision problem, not necessarily an array.

sections.title: Why feasibility permits elimination
paragraphs: For a minimum feasible answer, prove that if x works then every larger candidate works. A decision procedure Feasible(x) answers only yes/no. Then search for the first true candidate. “Minimize the maximum” is a clue, not proof; some objectives lack a monotone predicate or need a different decision algorithm.

Bounds must contain an answer. For ordered positive package weights, the smallest possible capacity is the heaviest package and the largest is the total weight. The upper bound is feasible for any positive day limit. All bounds and loads are long because the total can exceed int. Our nonnegative bounds make hi-lo safe.

sections.title: Shipping, split-array, and eating-speed variants
paragraphs: For a candidate shipping capacity, greedily load each day until the next package would exceed it, then start another day. Keeping each day as full as possible cannot increase the days needed for ordered positive packages. Stop early if the day limit is exceeded. The predicate takes O(n), so total cost is O(n log S) where S is the searched capacity range.

Splitting a nonnegative array into at most D contiguous groups uses the same greedy check. Negative elements invalidate that proof. Eating-speed tasks use a different check: total hours is the sum of ceiling(pile/speed), usually computed with long as (pile+speed-1)/speed, and feasibility compares it to available hours. Do not reuse shipping’s “current load” simulation for that task.

First demonstrate two candidates, one failing and one passing, before coding. If no candidate can succeed under the stated constraints, return a specified absence result rather than pretending the upper bound works.

guides.title: Intervals: merging, room counts, and greedy selection
guides.summary: Endpoint conventions decide whether equality is overlap.

sections.title: Sort by start to merge
paragraphs: Sort a copy by start. Maintain a result of disjoint merged intervals. The current interval either starts after the last result ends, creating a new component, or overlaps it, extending the end to the maximum. Never replace the end unconditionally: a nested interval may end earlier.

The provided merge treats intervals as closed, so [1,3] and [3,5] become [1,5]. Half-open intervals may use a different merge policy. Sorting dominates O(n log n) time; copying/output needs O(n) space. The comparator uses CompareTo, not subtraction that could overflow.

sections.title: Room count is maximum simultaneous occupancy
paragraphs: For half-open meetings [start,end), sort by start, remove all active ends <= the next start, insert its end, and track the maximum active count. At a timestamp shared by an end and a start, the room is reusable. Positive-duration validation makes zero-length ambiguity explicit.

A sweep-line alternative processes end events before start events on ties and tracks occupancy. A min-heap holds end times because the earliest-finishing active room is the next one that can become available. Time O(n log n), space O(n). A heap for selecting k largest has a different invariant despite using the same API.
sections.example: [1,3), [2,4), [3,5) need 2 rooms, because the first room is free at time 3.

sections.title: Maximum count: choose the earliest finish
paragraphs: Sort by end and take each interval whose start is at least the last chosen end. Exchange argument: replacing the first interval of any optimal solution with the earliest-ending candidate leaves at least as much room for everything after it. Repeat on the suffix.

This maximizes the number of compatible intervals, not total reward. Weighted scheduling can prefer one longer high-value interval and generally needs DP. The sample uses half-open positive-duration intervals and accepts touching endpoints. Time O(n log n); the scan itself is O(n).

guides.title: Grid BFS and multi-source spread
guides.summary: BFS explores increasing edge distance; mark discovery when you enqueue.

sections.title: Shortest path means equal-cost edges
paragraphs: Treat each traversable cell as a vertex and each allowed move as an edge. BFS uses a FIFO queue, so it processes all vertices at distance d before any at distance d+1. Mark a neighbor seen when enqueuing it. Its first discovery is therefore by a shortest path, and it enters the queue once.

The supplied method returns edge count: source==target is 0, adjacent cells are distance 1, and unreachable is -1. It accepts a rectangular jagged grid with 0=open and any other value=blocked, does not mutate it, and checks both endpoints. Capture queue.Count before each level loop; otherwise newly enqueued cells leak into the current distance.

DFS can find a path, but its first found path need not be shortest. BFS’s guarantee needs equal edge costs. Arbitrary nonnegative weights need Dijkstra; zero/one weights can use 0-1 BFS. A cell count along a path is edge distance+1 for a reachable nonempty path, so never silently swap these conventions. O(rows×columns) time and space.
sections.example: In [[0,0],[1,0]], from (0,0) to (1,1), the shortest path has 2 edges and 3 cells.

sections.title: All sources belong to distance zero
paragraphs: For simultaneous spread, enqueue every initial source before the first BFS level. This finds distance to the nearest source rather than running separate searches. RottingMinutes counts fresh cells, marks them rotten at enqueue time, and advances minutes only while fresh cells remain.

With no fresh cells the answer is zero even if there are no initial sources. If fresh cells remain after the queue empties, return -1. Input mutation is explicit here because rotten state doubles as visited state. For nearest-source distances without mutation, store a distance grid initialized to -1.
sections.example: [2,1,1,2] finishes in 1 minute: both sources expand simultaneously, not one after the other.

sections.title: Discovery-time marking prevents repeated work
paragraphs: If two current cells can both reach the same neighbor, late marking can enqueue that neighbor twice, potentially propagating many duplicate entries. Mark when the work item is created, not when it is removed. For DFS, the equivalent is marking before recursive calls or when pushing onto a stack.

In-place marking saves a separate visited array but changes the caller’s data. Ask whether mutation is allowed, or use seen. Some searches need state beyond a coordinate (for example, coordinate plus remaining eliminations); in those cases “seen cell” alone is insufficient.

guides.title: Flood fill and iterative DFS

sections.title: Counting islands
paragraphs: Scan every grid cell. Whenever unvisited land is found, increment the island count and exhaustively explore that land component before continuing the scan. Every future land cell in that component is already marked, so it cannot increment the answer again. Orthogonal and diagonal connectivity are different problem definitions; the sample uses four directions.

The code replaces land “1” with water “0” when scheduling the cell and uses an explicit stack. This mutates the input and needs O(rows×columns) worst-case stack space. A separate visited grid preserves input but uses additional storage. Total time is O(rows×columns): each cell has only four possible neighbors.

Recursive DFS is shorter, but the call stack can grow with component size, not merely with grid height. A one-cell-wide winding island can create a very deep call chain. guides.title: Dependency graphs and topological order
guides.summary: Only emit a node after every prerequisite has been emitted.

sections.title: Kahn’s algorithm
paragraphs: For each directed edge prerequisite→dependent, increment the dependent’s indegree and add it to the prerequisite’s outgoing neighbors. Initially queue all zero-indegree vertices. Emitting a vertex removes its outgoing edges conceptually, decrementing indegrees; a neighbor enters the queue exactly when its indegree reaches zero.

The invariant is that queued vertices have no remaining unmet prerequisites. If all n vertices are emitted, their order is valid. If fewer are emitted, the remaining directed subgraph contains a cycle, so no complete order exists. Include isolated vertices by allocating all n nodes, not just those appearing in edges.

Input formats frequently list (course,prerequisite), while this method expects (prerequisite,dependent). Convert that orientation explicitly. Duplicate edges are represented and counted consistently here. Multiple valid orders may exist; queue order chooses one, while a priority queue can enforce smallest-ID order if required. O(V+E) time and space.
sections.example: Edges 0→2 and 1→2 allow [0,1,2] or [1,0,2]. Adding 2→0 creates a cycle involving 0 and 2.

sections.title: Directed-cycle detection differs from undirected connectivity
paragraphs: Kahn detects directed cycles by incomplete output. A DFS alternative uses three colors: unseen, active on the current recursion path, and finished. An edge to an active node is a back edge and proves a cycle; an edge to a finished node does not. A boolean visited set alone cannot distinguish those cases.

Union-Find answers undirected connectivity and detects a cycle when an undirected insertion connects vertices already joined. It is not a general directed-cycle detector. Also distinguish a dependency cycle from a strongly connected component query: a yes/no cycle answer does not list every cyclic group.

guides.title: Union-Find for undirected connectivity
guides.summary: Represent each component by one root and make unions cheap.

sections.title: Roots, compression, and size
paragraphs: Every vertex initially points to itself. Find follows parent links to a representative root. Union finds both representatives; if different, attach the smaller tree under the larger root and add their sizes. If equal, the vertices were already connected. Maintain a component count by decrementing only on successful unions.

Path compression shortens future traversals. The sample uses path halving: each visited node points to its grandparent while walking to the root. Pairing compression with union by size gives near-constant amortized operations, conventionally O(α(n)); it is not a guarantee that each individual operation takes exactly one step. Initialization and storage are O(n).

For incremental undirected edges, a failed union means the new edge closes a cycle (including a repeated edge under multigraph semantics). For accounts merge, map each shared identity to an owner index and union owners, then collect records by representative. This structure does not support arbitrary edge deletions, path reconstruction, or directed reachability.

For a one-time static component count, a DFS/BFS adjacency list is often simpler. Union-Find shines when connectivity evolves through many additions. Roots are implementation representatives, not necessarily the smallest IDs or meaningful domain leaders.

guides.title: Shortest paths with nonnegative weights
guides.summary: Finalize the smallest currently known distance, and ignore stale heap entries.

sections.title: Distances are best known path costs
paragraphs: Initialize the source distance to zero and every other vertex to infinity. Remove the smallest-distance item from a min-heap and relax each outgoing edge: if distance[u]+weight improves distance[v], store the improvement and enqueue it. Nonnegative edges are essential to the greedy argument: no later detour can reduce a finalized shortest distance.

The .NET priority queue has no decrease-key operation, so the sample enqueues a new entry for each improvement. Old entries remain; skip a popped entry if its distance differs from the currently stored best distance. Strict improvement prevents repeated enqueueing on zero-cost cycles. The code uses long distances and int nonnegative weights, and never adds to the infinity sentinel.

The result gives distances, not routes. To reconstruct a route, update predecessor[v]=u whenever relaxing, then walk backward from the destination. Unreachable vertices remain long.MaxValue. With lazy heap duplicates the usual bound is O((V+E) log E) time and O(V+E) storage; for ordinary simple graphs it is commonly written O((V+E) log V).
sections.example: Edges 0→1 cost 8, 0→2 cost 2, 2→1 cost 1: distance to 1 improves from 8 to 3; its old heap entry at 8 is stale.

sections.title: Choosing the path algorithm
paragraphs: Equal edge costs: BFS. Nonnegative weights: Dijkstra. A directed acyclic graph can use topological-order relaxation even with negative weights. General negative-weight edges may require Bellman-Ford and reachable negative-cycle detection. If a reachable negative cycle can lead to the destination, there is no finite minimum path cost.

Do not choose solely from the word “weighted.” Confirm whether the objective is sum of edge weights, maximum edge effort, number of stops, or something else. Additional constraints can require a richer state such as (vertex,stopsUsed); a single best distance per vertex may then discard needed paths.

guides.title: Backtracking: enumerate choices and undo local state
guides.summary: Each recursive path represents one partial candidate.

sections.title: Subsets, combinations, and permutations
paragraphs: For subsets, record the current path, then try each remaining index as the next choice. Recursing with i+1 prevents picking the same position twice and avoids generating the same subset in different orders. For fixed-size combinations, record only at the target length. For permutations, each level may choose any unused position, so use a used array rather than a monotonically increasing start index.

The invariant is that path contains exactly the choices made along the active call chain. Choose, recurse, then undo before trying the next sibling. If duplicate input values should produce unique outputs, sort and skip equal sibling choices; position-distinct output is a different contract. Prune only when you can prove a partial candidate cannot lead to a valid result.

Materializing all subsets inherently costs O(n·2^n) output time/space because there are 2^n subsets and copying has a length cost. The recursion/path overhead excluding output is O(n). An exponential algorithm is sometimes required by exponential output, but large-n enumeration is still impractical.

sections.title: Why the output must copy the path
paragraphs: A List is a mutable reference object. Adding the same path object to results repeatedly stores aliases, not snapshots. Later RemoveAt calls mutate every “result,” often leaving them all empty. path.ToArray() or new List<int>(path) creates an independent snapshot.

Restoring state is equally important when returning early. For a boolean search, ensure used flags are restored before returning success if the caller may reuse that data. The word-search sample restores its local visited state and never changes the board.
sections.example: For [1,2], independent subset snapshots are [], [1], [1,2], [2]; four references to one mutable list are not four answers.

sections.title: Word search: visited belongs to the current path
paragraphs: Try every board cell as a starting point. A state (row,column,index) must match the next character and cannot reuse a cell already on the active path. Mark before visiting neighbors and unmark on return. A global visited set would incorrectly forbid a cell that failed in an unrelated path.

The sample uses a separate bool grid rather than overwriting a character with a sentinel, so it works for any char value and preserves the board. Four-direction movement is explicit. Empty word returns true; insufficient board cells returns false. Worst-case search is exponential in word length, loosely O(rows·columns·4^L), with O(rows·columns+L) auxiliary space here. sections.title: Generate only valid parentheses prefixes
paragraphs: Track opens and closes used. Add an opening bracket if opens<n. Add a closing bracket only if closes<opens. These conditions preserve two invariants: no prefix closes more brackets than it opened, and neither count exceeds n. At length 2n, the constructed string is valid.

A fixed char buffer avoids repeated string concatenation; copy it with new string(buffer) only at a complete answer. For n=0, the one valid construction is the empty string. Output count follows Catalan growth, so complexity is proportional to output length, O(n·Catalan(n)); auxiliary recursion/buffer space excluding output is O(n). Small n is a genuine requirement.

guides.title: A trie for prefixes and whole words

sections.title: Insert, exact search, and prefix search
paragraphs: Starting at a root with no character of its own, follow one child edge per input character. Insert allocates missing nodes and marks the final node as a complete word. Prefix search succeeds whenever the walk exists. Exact search also requires the final End flag, because an existing path may be only a prefix of a longer word.

An array of 26 children trades predictable lookup for per-node memory and requires lowercase ASCII a-z. Validate the whole word before modifying the trie, so invalid input cannot leave a partial insertion. A dictionary of children supports a broader/sparse alphabet but adds hashing and allocation costs.

Insert and lookup cost O(L) for a word of length L; total nodes are bounded by total inserted characters plus the root. Empty prefix always exists; inserting an empty word sets root.End and makes exact empty-word search succeed. The null-coalescing assignment creates a child only if missing.

A trie is useful for many shared-prefix queries, autocomplete traversal, and dictionary-based backtracking. For only exact membership, a HashSet<string> is often simpler. Enumerating autocomplete suggestions also pays for all visited suffix nodes and emitted strings; it is not just O(prefix length).

guides.title: One-dimensional DP: define the state first
guides.summary: A recurrence is a claim about a precise subproblem, not a formula to memorize.

sections.title: Counting ways to reach step n
paragraphs: Define ways[i] as the number of ordered sequences of 1-step and 2-step moves reaching i. The final move comes from i-1 or i-2, two disjoint possibilities, so ways[i]=ways[i-1]+ways[i-2]. Set ways[0]=1 for the empty sequence and ways[1]=1. These base cases are part of the model, not arbitrary initialization.

Only two preceding states are needed, so roll them forward. The supplied implementation uses BigInteger because counts quickly exceed int and long. It performs O(n) additions with O(1) stored numbers, but arbitrary-precision numbers grow in bit length, so bit-level cost and storage are not constant. A fixed-width version needs a documented n bound or checked overflow.

sections.title: Minimum cost is a different state
paragraphs: For stair cost, define dp[i] as minimum cost to stand just beyond the first i stairs, with starts at 0 or 1 permitted. To reach i, pay cost[i-1] from i-1 or cost[i-2] from i-2. Thus dp[i]=min(dp[i-1]+cost[i-1],dp[i-2]+cost[i-2]), with dp[0]=dp[1]=0.

“Minimum cost” and “maximum profit” do not identify one universal recurrence. Write what i represents, what the last decision is, what values can transition into i, and whether the answer is dp[n] or a maximum across states. Then check every boundary before compressing memory.
sections.example: Costs [10,15,20]: start at step 1 and pay 15, then leave the stairs; minimum cost is 15.

sections.title: No adjacent picks
paragraphs: For each value, either skip it and keep the best previous prefix, or take it and add the best prefix ending two positions earlier. Keep twoBack and oneBack before updating them. This preserves the meaning of old states while computing the new state.

The sample allows choosing no elements, so empty or all-negative input gives zero. If the prompt requires at least one selection, this base case must change. Time O(n), fixed-width auxiliary space O(1). A circular arrangement requires excluding either the first or the last position and taking the better linear result.

guides.title: Coin change and DP iteration direction
guides.summary: The loop order encodes whether a choice can be reused.

sections.title: Fewest coins with unlimited reuse
paragraphs: Define dp[amount] as the minimum coins needed for exactly that amount. dp[0]=0. For each total, try every positive coin no larger than total: a solution can end with that coin after an optimal solution for total-coin. Use a bounded unreachable sentinel and return -1 if the target remains unreachable.

The provided amount-outer implementation computes smaller totals first, so repeated denominations are naturally allowed. Time O(amount×numberOfCoins), memory O(amount). This is pseudopolynomial: it depends on numeric amount, not merely the number of bits encoding it. Very large amounts can make this approach impractical.

A greedy largest-coin-first solution is not generally correct. With coins [1,3,4] and amount 6, greedy uses 4+1+1 while DP finds 3+3. A zero or negative denomination breaks progress and must be rejected.

sections.title: Each item once versus reusable items
paragraphs: For a one-dimensional 0/1 knapsack or subset-sum table, process capacities downward for each item. Then dp[capacity-item] still represents the previous item layer, preventing the same item from being reused within its own iteration. An upward loop reads cells already updated by this item and enables unlimited reuse.

Counting combinations versus ordered sequences also changes loop order: coins outer then amount ascending counts unordered coin combinations under a distinct-denomination contract; amount outer then coins counts ordered sequences. Minimization and counting cannot be swapped without revisiting state and duplicates. The general rule is to draw dependencies and decide which logical layer each read must use.

guides.summary: A subsequence may skip positions; a substring may not.

sections.title: Longest strictly increasing subsequence
paragraphs: The straightforward DP defines dp[i] as the longest increasing subsequence ending at i. Try each j<i with values[j]<values[i], then dp[i]=max(dp[i],dp[j]+1). This O(n²) version is often easiest to derive and explain.

The faster method stores tails[len-1], the smallest possible final value of any increasing subsequence of that length. Replace the first tail >= current value using lower bound, or append if none exists. Smaller tails leave more room for future extension. The tails array is an optimization summary and may not itself be a valid subsequence; reconstruction needs predecessor information.
Strictly increasing uses first >=; nondecreasing uses first >. Empty input yields zero. Time O(n log n), space O(n).
sections.example: [3,1,2] changes tails [3]→[1]→[1,2], yielding length 2.

sections.title: Edit distance, LCS, and interleaving
paragraphs: For edit distance, dp[i,j] is the minimum edits turning the first i code units of a into the first j of b. Empty-prefix base cases are dp[i,0]=i and dp[0,j]=j. Equal final symbols reuse the diagonal; otherwise take one plus the minimum of replace (diagonal), delete (above), and insert (left). The sample uses unit costs.

LCS uses a different recurrence: equal symbols give 1+diagonal, otherwise max of skipping one side. Interleaving is boolean: dp[i,j] means the first i+j target symbols can be formed from the two prefixes, with transitions matching the target’s next symbol. A shared table shape does not mean shared initialization or operators.

These methods need O(mn) states and O(1) work per state. Full tables use O(mn) space; rolling rows can reduce storage after you understand which previous cells are required. The memoized LCS example shows top-down caching but has recursion depth up to O(m+n), which may require an iterative alternative.

sections.title: Unique paths and minimum path sum
paragraphs: For right/down movement, every path to a cell comes from above or left. Counting paths therefore adds the two predecessor counts. A one-row table initially represents the previous row; as you move left to right, dp[c] is “above” and dp[c-1] has become “left in the current row.” This is a deliberate dependency order.

Set dp[0]=1 and all other cells to zero before scanning all rows. The supplied method uses BigInteger and returns zero if either dimension is zero. If there are obstacles, set dp[c]=0 when that cell is blocked. For minimum path sum, replace addition of counts by min(above,left)+cellCost and handle the first row/column explicitly.

The state and recurrence rely on acyclic allowed moves. If you can move in all four directions or revisit cells, a simple one-pass DP is not valid; use a graph formulation with suitable costs. Negative cell values are not a problem for a right/down DAG but can matter greatly in a cyclic graph.
For fixed-width arithmetic the scan is O(rows×columns) time and O(columns) space; BigInteger arithmetic also depends on count bit length. Do not claim a universal int bound for path counts.

guides.title: Tree traversals: return values, levels, and ancestors
guides.summary: Decide whether information flows down, up, or level by level.

sections.title: DFS returns a fact about a subtree
paragraphs: For depth measured in nodes, an empty subtree has depth zero. Recursively obtain left and right depths, then return one plus their maximum. The contract of each recursive call is the key: callers do not need to know how the child computed its answer.

Other tree problems change the returned fact. Diameter may return height to the parent while updating a global best path through each node. Path-sum questions may pass an accumulated or remaining sum downward. Do not confuse a global answer with the per-subtree return value. Traversal costs O(n), and recursion uses O(h) stack where h can equal n for a skewed tree.
sections.example: A single node has depth 1 in this API; depth in edges would instead be 0 and requires different base-case conventions.

sections.title: BFS levels, right view, and zigzag
paragraphs: Capture the queue size at the start of a level and process exactly that many nodes. Child nodes are queued for the next level. Recording each value yields level order. The right-side view records the last value of each level when children are enqueued left before right.

For zigzag output, keep traversal normal and place each value at i or size-1-i depending on level parity. This separates visitation from output order. Empty trees return an empty result. Time O(n), queue space O(maximum width), plus output. The convenience RightSideView method below reuses materialized Levels, so that particular implementation retains O(n) level data; a direct per-level last-node implementation can avoid that extra materialization. A wide balanced tree can make BFS’s queue larger than DFS’s recursion stack.

sections.title: Lowest common ancestor
paragraphs: In a general binary tree, return the current node if it is either target reference. Otherwise ask both subtrees. If both return a non-null match, the current node is the split point; if only one does, propagate that match upward. This concise version assumes both targets exist in the tree and identity is based on references.

If a target might be absent, add presence validation or return a match count alongside the candidate; otherwise a single present target can be mistaken for an LCA of both. For a BST with unique keys and known-present targets, walk left while both keys are smaller, right while both are larger, and stop at the split. General-tree time is O(n), BST time O(h).
sections.example: In root 5 with descendants 2 and 8 on opposite sides, their LCA is 5. A node is its own ancestor under this convention.

guides.title: BST validation and ordered traversal
guides.summary: The BST rule is inherited from every ancestor, not just the parent.

sections.title: Carry the legal range
paragraphs: In a strict BST, every node in a left subtree must be below its ancestor and every node in a right subtree must be above it. Carry exclusive lower and upper bounds downward. Going left tightens the upper bound to the current value; going right tightens the lower bound. Checking only the parent-child pair misses deep violations.

The supplied iterative validator uses long bounds for int node values, so int.MinValue and int.MaxValue are both legitimate keys. Duplicate values are rejected by the strict inequalities. If duplicates are permitted, define which side owns them and adapt the bound inclusivity consistently. Time O(n), explicit stack O(h) worst-case.
sections.example: Root 10, left child 5, and 5’s right child 12 passes local parent checks but violates the inherited upper bound 10.

sections.title: In-order visits sorted keys
paragraphs: An in-order walk visits left subtree, node, right subtree. In a valid BST this is sorted order, so decrement a 1-based k at each visited node and return when it reaches zero. The iterative stack stores unfinished ancestors while walking left.

If k is invalid, the sample throws rather than returning an ambiguous integer sentinel. A null tree cannot have a kth element. Runtime is O(h+k) to reach an existing kth item, O(n) worst case, and stack O(h). For repeated rank queries on a changing tree, maintained subtree sizes enable order-statistic operations, but that is beyond the basic one-query interview solution.

guides.summary: Values alone cannot tell a parser where children are missing.

sections.title: A grammar for the tree
paragraphs: Define the encoding recursively: a null node is “#”; a non-null node is its integer value followed by its left encoding and right encoding, separated by commas. Preorder plus null markers uniquely specifies both values and shape. Without null markers, a single-child-left tree and a single-child-right tree can have the same value sequence.

Deserialization keeps a cursor into the token stream. Read one token: null marker returns null; otherwise parse a value, then consume exactly one left subtree and one right subtree in that order. Reject premature end and trailing tokens so malformed data cannot be silently accepted.

The supplied code uses invariant culture for integer formatting/parsing, supports negative values, and represents the empty tree as “#”. Serialization and parsing take O(n) tokens, plus output length; recursive stack O(h). Very tall or untrusted trees can overflow recursion or allocate excessive memory, so production parsers need depth/size limits or iterative state.

Round-trip tests should compare structure and values, not only serialized length. Also test malformed “1,#” and trailing “#,#”. Delimiters are safe here because payloads are integers; arbitrary strings would need escaping, length prefixes, or a standard structured format.

guides.summary: Separate geometry from data mutation.

sections.title: Spiral traversal and clockwise rotation
paragraphs: Spiral traversal keeps top, bottom, left, and right boundaries of the unvisited rectangle. Emit its top row and right column, shrink those boundaries, then emit bottom and left only if their bounds still describe unvisited cells. Those guards prevent duplicate visits on a single remaining row or column.

A 90-degree clockwise rotation of a square matrix can be decomposed into a transpose followed by reversing every row. Transpose swaps only above-diagonal pairs so each pair moves once. This is an in-place O(n²) operation with O(1) extra space; a nonsquare matrix needs a new shape/output allocation.

The sample validates rectangular jagged arrays before either operation. Spiral is O(rows×columns) time and O(output size) storage. Empty and zero-column grids return empty. Check a one-row grid, a one-column grid, and an odd square to expose boundary errors.
sections.example: [[1,2],[3,4]] spirals to [1,2,4,3] and rotates clockwise to [[3,1],[4,2]].

sections.title: First-row/column markers
paragraphs: To zero every row and column containing an original zero, use the first row and first column as marker storage. First remember whether either originally contains a zero, using two flags. Scan only the interior to write markers; then scan the interior again to apply them. Finally zero the first row and column according to the saved flags.

Writing zeros immediately during the discovery scan would create new zeros that falsely trigger additional rows and columns. Keeping detection separate from application preserves the original-data meaning. This method intentionally mutates the matrix, costs O(rows×columns) time, and uses O(1) auxiliary space. A separate row/column set is simpler when constant extra space is unnecessary.

guides.title: Array invariants: duplicate, majority, and products
guides.summary: Special constraints make these linear-time shortcuts possible.

sections.title: Values as next indices
paragraphs: With n+1 entries whose values are all in 1..n and exactly one distinct duplicated value, define next(index)=values[index]. Starting from index zero reaches a cycle. Its entry corresponds to the duplicated value because multiple links converge there. Floyd’s meeting phase and reset phase find that entry without changing the array.

These exact constraints matter. Arbitrary integers cannot be used as indices, and a different duplicate model may not meet the promised output. The sample validates ranges but assumes the unique-duplicate contract rather than scanning with extra memory. Time O(n), auxiliary space O(1). This is a specialized technique, not a default replacement for a HashSet.
sections.example: [1,3,4,2,2] follows 0→1→3→2→4→2; entry value 2 is the duplicate.

sections.title: Cancellation leaves a majority candidate
paragraphs: Boyer-Moore voting pairs unequal values and cancels them. A value appearing more than half the time cannot be completely canceled by all other values combined. Track a candidate and a balance; when balance is zero choose the next value as candidate.

The surviving candidate is not proof that a majority exists. Unless existence is guaranteed, make a second counting pass and return absence when frequency<=n/2. The sample returns nullable int, including null for empty input. O(n) time and O(1) space. General “most frequent” is a different problem.

sections.title: Prefix products times suffix products
paragraphs: For index i, multiply all values strictly before i and all values strictly after i. First write exclusive prefix products into the output. Then sweep backward with one suffix product and multiply it into each output slot. This handles zeros without division, including two zeros producing all-zero output.

The sample returns long[] and uses checked multiplication: all intermediate products must fit long. Empty returns empty; a singleton returns [1], the empty product. Auxiliary space excluding output is O(1), time O(n). If arbitrary large products are required, use BigInteger and account for bit-level cost.

guides.title: LRU cache and a minimum stack
guides.summary: Combine structures so each operation has the information it needs.

sections.title: LRU: index plus recency list
paragraphs: A dictionary maps each key directly to a linked-list node. The doubly linked list orders nodes from most recent at the front to least recent at the back. A hit moves that exact node to the front. An update changes its value and also moves it. A new insertion goes at the front; if capacity is exceeded, remove the last node from both structures.

The invariant is a one-to-one relationship between dictionary entries and list nodes, with every key appearing once. Storing only a value in the dictionary would force a linear search to find its list position. Expected lookup and mutation are O(1), with O(capacity) retained space.

The sample uses TryGet to distinguish a missing key from a stored sentinel value. Capacity zero stores nothing. It is intentionally single-threaded; a production cache needs concurrency coordination, lifetime/eviction semantics, and possibly memory accounting. Do not claim that wrapping only the dictionary in a concurrent type makes the combined structure thread-safe.
sections.example: Capacity 2: Put(1), Put(2), Get(1), Put(3) evicts 2 because accessing 1 refreshed its recency.

sections.title: Record the running minimum with each value
paragraphs: Each stack entry stores its own value and the minimum of all entries at or below it. Push computes min(newValue,previousMin); Pop removes both together. Therefore the remaining top always knows the current minimum, including repeated equal minimum values.

A separate synchronized minimum stack is equivalent, but paired entries make the invariant hard to break. Push, Pop, Peek, and Minimum are O(1) amortized where resizing applies; storage O(n). The sample throws on empty Pop/Peek/Minimum through the underlying Stack API, rather than returning a valid value that could be confused with absence.

guides.title: Greedy decisions and maximum-subarray state
guides.summary: Keep a proof of what can safely be forgotten.

sections.title: One stock trade: best buy so far
paragraphs: For each potential selling day, the best earlier buy is the lowest price seen so far. Keep that minimum and the largest observed sell-minus-buy difference. Updating the minimum first allows a zero-length “no profitable trade” candidate, which matches the at-most-one-trade contract.

The discarded prices cannot beat a cheaper earlier buy for a future sale. That dominance argument is the greedy proof. Empty or monotonically falling prices return zero. Widen arithmetic to long. Multiple trades, fees, cooldowns, or position constraints change the state and cannot be solved by blindly reusing this one-trade formula.

sections.title: Kadane’s algorithm is a small DP
paragraphs: Define endingHere as the best nonempty contiguous subarray ending at the current position. Either extend the previous subarray or start at the current element. Keep a separate global best because the optimal subarray may end before the last position.

Initialize from the first value rather than zero so all-negative input returns the largest negative value. Empty input is rejected under the nonempty contract. O(n) time, O(1) fixed-width extra space. This solves contiguous subarray sum, not arbitrary subsequence selection.
sections.example: [-4,-2,-7] returns -2, not 0; [4,-1,2] returns 5.

sections.title: Jump-game reachable frontier
paragraphs: Keep the farthest index reachable using positions already scanned. If the next index exceeds that frontier, no explored position can get you there, so the reachable region cannot expand further. Otherwise update the frontier with index+maximumJump.

This greedy summary answers reachability because reaching a position earlier does not consume a resource needed later. It does not automatically yield a minimum jump count or a path. Use long for index+jump and validate nonnegative jumps.

guides.title: Bit operations with narrow, useful contracts
guides.summary: Learn XOR cancellation and clear-lowest-bit before specialized bit tricks.

sections.title: XOR for one unpaired value
paragraphs: XOR is associative and commutative, x XOR x is zero, and x XOR zero is x. If every value occurs exactly twice except one, XORing the array cancels all paired values and leaves the singleton. No arithmetic overflow occurs because XOR acts on bits.

This contract is narrower than “find a unique value.” Values occurring three times or two separate singletons need different reasoning. The sample does not validate occurrence counts; that would require more work or memory. Empty input returns zero from the identity operation but does not satisfy the promised singleton contract. O(n) time, O(1) space.

sections.title: Clear the lowest set bit
paragraphs: For a nonzero unsigned integer x, subtracting one flips the lowest one bit to zero and lower zeros to ones. x & (x-1) therefore clears exactly the lowest set bit. Repeat until zero to count set bits. A uint contract avoids confusing arithmetic right-shift behavior on negative signed numbers.

The loop runs once per set bit, at most 32 times for uint. A fixed-width built-in such as BitOperations.PopCount is preferable when permitted; understanding the invariant is still useful. C# shift counts are masked to the operand width, so shifting an int by 32 does not mean a 33-bit value. Do not use bitmask subset enumeration for large n without checking exponential output and width.
sections.example: 12 is binary 1100: 12 & 11 = 8 (1000), then 8 & 7 = 0, so two bits.
