guides.title: C# queue, stack, deque, and heap APIs
guides.summary: Choose removal order first, then the collection.

sections.title: PriorityQueue is a min-heap
paragraphs: PriorityQueue<TElement,TPriority> removes the element with the lowest priority under its comparer. Enqueue accepts payload and priority separately. Dequeue returns only the payload; TryDequeue also gives the priority and returns false if empty. Peek does not remove. Equal priorities are not guaranteed FIFO.

Heap insertion/removal costs O(log n), root access O(1). Enumeration is not sorted order. The complete example’s MinHeapRoot enqueues string payloads with integer priorities and verifies the earlier-priority item is removed first.

sections.title: Max-heap without negation overflow
paragraphs: Construct PriorityQueue<int,int> with Comparer<int>.Create((a,b)=>b.CompareTo(a)). Reversing comparison changes priority order without arithmetic. Do not write b-a: subtraction can overflow and violate comparison ordering. Negating priorities also fails at int.MinValue unless you widen first.

MaxHeapRoot handles int.MinValue and int.MaxValue without special cases. The queue compares priorities, not payloads, so changing only the payload does not affect ordering. Use the same comparer interpretation in every enqueue and dequeue.

sections.title: FIFO queue
paragraphs: Enqueue appends; Dequeue removes the oldest element; Peek reads it; Count reports queued elements. TryDequeue avoids an empty-queue exception when absence is expected. Enqueue is amortized O(1), and normal dequeue is O(1). Use Queue<T> for BFS so earlier discoveries leave before later discoveries.

During level BFS, capture Count before the inner loop. Count changes as items are removed and children added. Ordinary Queue<T> is not a concurrent work queue; thread safety requires a different design or synchronization.

sections.title: Stack<T>: use the most recently added item first
paragraphs: A stack is a collection that gives you the most recently added item first, like taking the top plate from a pile. This is called last in, first out, or LIFO. The “top” is the latest item still in the stack, not the largest value. Stack<int> stores integers; Stack<char> stores characters.

Push(x) adds x at the top. Pop() removes the top item and returns it. Peek() returns the top item without removing it. Count tells you how many items remain. If you push 10 and then 20, Peek returns 20 and Count is still 2. Pop then returns 20, leaving 10 as the top and Count equal to 1.

Pop and Peek throw InvalidOperationException if the stack is empty, so check Count > 0 first when emptiness is possible. Alternatively, TryPop(out item) returns false on an empty stack; when it returns true, item contains the value it removed. TryPeek does the same without removing the item. The complete example below can be called as StackBasics.Demonstrate().

Use a stack when the most recent unfinished item is the next one you must handle, such as undoing the latest action or closing an inner bracket pair before the outer pair. An array or List<T> is more suitable when you need arbitrary positions. The “Stacks, from the beginning” guide in the coding guide library walks through the bracket example before introducing next-greater problems.

Pop, Peek, and Count take O(1), or constant time. Push is usually constant time, but occasionally C# grows the internal storage and copies existing items. Over many pushes, the average work per push is O(1); this is called amortized O(1). A stack changes removal order, not the objects it holds: if it contains references, those references still point to the same objects.

sections.title: Both ends with LinkedList<T>
paragraphs: In the .NET 8 baseline used here, LinkedList<T> provides deque behavior through AddFirst/AddLast and RemoveFirst/RemoveLast. First and Last are nullable node references; check Count or null before reading Value. These endpoint operations are O(1).

A linked list allocates nodes and has poorer locality than an array-backed ring buffer. It is adequate for interview clarity; a purpose-built deque can be better for performance. Do not confuse removing a known node (O(1)) with finding a node by value (O(n)).

guides.title: C# maps, sets, ordered keys, and iteration
guides.summary: Lookup semantics matter as much as the method names.

sections.title: TryGetValue and missing defaults
paragraphs: TryGetValue performs one lookup and separately tells you whether a key exists. The out value is default when missing, so do not infer presence from the value itself: zero may be a real stored value. ContainsKey followed by the indexer is valid but performs repeated lookup when you also need the value.

GetValueOrDefault is convenient when a missing value should equal a chosen default, such as a frequency of zero. It does not insert. Expected dictionary lookup is O(1), with cost also depending on hashing/equality of the key; hashing a long string is not free.

sections.title: Incrementing a frequency map
paragraphs: Read the previous frequency (zero if absent), then assign previous+1. The complete Frequencies method demonstrates TryGetValue; counts[c]=counts.GetValueOrDefault(c)+1 is the compact equivalent. An indexer assignment inserts a missing key or replaces an existing value.

For a sliding window, decrement on removal and delete zero-count keys if dictionary.Count represents current distinct symbols. For counting arbitrarily large streams, int counts can overflow; a bounded in-memory string has an int length, so its per-character count fits int.

sections.title: HashSet is membership with uniqueness
paragraphs: HashSet<T>.Add returns true only when the value was absent. That makes if(seen.Add(value)) useful for discovery-time work. Contains checks membership and Remove reports whether an element was removed. It stores no multiplicity, so it cannot replace a frequency map in a counting problem.

Equality comparers define uniqueness. For string identifiers, explicitly choose ordinal or another required comparer rather than accidentally implementing a different case policy. Expected Add/Contains/Remove cost O(1), retained memory O(distinct items).

sections.title: SortedSet and SortedDictionary
paragraphs: SortedSet<T> stores unique values in comparer order; SortedDictionary<TKey,TValue> stores keys in comparer order. Typical lookup/insertion/removal costs O(log n). Use them when you need ordered iteration or range-related operations, not merely because a problem mentions sorting once.

The comparer decides when keys are equal for ordering, so it must be consistent and transitive. The sample uses StringComparer.Ordinal for ordered string keys. Min/Max may require walking a tree path and should not be assumed O(1). An unordered dictionary plus a one-time sort may be simpler for a final sorted report.

sections.title: Do not rely on a blanket enumeration rule
paragraphs: Many structural modifications invalidate a collection’s enumerator, but behavior depends on the collection, operation, and runtime version. Modern Dictionary implementations permit some removals/clears without invalidating enumeration; adding elements is still not a generally safe enumeration strategy.

A portable interview pattern is to snapshot the keys (new List<string>(dictionary.Keys)), iterate that stable snapshot, and perform planned removals on the dictionary. This adds O(n) memory and time for the copy. Alternatively collect removals first and apply them after enumeration. Do not mutate the copied list while enumerating it either.

guides.summary: Know what the library mutates and what its return value means.

sections.title: Sorting intervals by a key
paragraphs: Use Array.Sort(intervals,(a,b)=>a[0].CompareTo(b[0])) to order by start. For List<T>, use list.Sort with the same comparator. CompareTo avoids the overflow risk of a[0]-b[0]. If equal-start ordering matters, add an end-value tie-breaker instead of relying on sort stability.

Array.Sort mutates the outer array. The sample clones that outer array first, preserving input order but sharing inner interval rows; changing a row afterward still affects the original. A deep copy is needed if you plan to mutate the interval values. Sorting costs O(n log n) comparisons.

sections.title: Descending order
paragraphs: Array.Sort followed by Array.Reverse gives descending order in place. A reverse comparer is another option. OrderByDescending(...).ToArray() creates a materialized sorted result and requires System.Linq; leaving off ToArray produces a deferred enumerable rather than an array.

Use a copy when preserving input order matters, and account for that allocation. Sorting to find one maximum is unnecessary O(n log n) work when a single O(n) scan suffices. Decide whether the goal is one extremum, top-k, or complete ordering before selecting the tool.

sections.title: Negative return is a complemented insertion point
paragraphs: Array.BinarySearch assumes the array is sorted under a compatible comparer. A nonnegative result is an index containing an equal value. A negative result encodes the insertion point with bitwise complement: apply ~result to recover it. It is not simply -result.

For duplicate values, a successful search may return any matching occurrence; it is not a lower-bound operation. Use a custom boundary search when the first/last occurrence is required. The sample FindOrInsertionPoint deliberately combines “a found index” and “an insertion point” into one result and documents that ambiguity.

guides.title: C# text construction and character contracts
guides.summary: A char is one UTF-16 code unit, not every possible human character.

sections.title: Building a string incrementally
paragraphs: Strings are immutable. Repeatedly appending to a growing string in a loop can copy the accumulated prefix each time, leading to quadratic total character copying. StringBuilder keeps a mutable buffer structure; Append adds pieces, and ToString produces the final immutable string.

This is a practical default for many incremental appends, not a ban on every use of +. A small fixed concatenation or interpolation is clearer and can be optimized by the compiler/runtime. If you already have all pieces, string.Join is usually simpler. Pre-sizing the builder can reduce resizing when a reliable length is known.

sections.title: Lowercase indexing requires an alphabet promise
paragraphs: c-'a' maps lowercase ASCII a-z to 0..25 because those code values are contiguous. Reverse with (char)('a'+index). Validate the character or index before indexing a 26-element array. Uppercase letters, accented letters, and arbitrary Unicode text violate that contract.

C# char and string indexing operate on UTF-16 code units. A Unicode scalar can span two chars, and a displayed grapheme may span several scalars. Clarify whether the interview guarantees lowercase English letters, ASCII, Unicode scalars, or user-perceived characters; the required representation changes accordingly.

sections.title: Join versus constructing from characters
paragraphs: string.Join(separator,values) formats a collection with separators. new string(charArray) creates a string from consecutive characters, and s.ToCharArray() creates a mutable copy of a string’s UTF-16 units. These allocate output/copies; they are not zero-cost views.

Reversing char units can split surrogate pairs or reverse combining marks, so ArrayStringApis.ReverseCopy is a code-unit reversal demonstration, not a general international-text reversal. If a question asks to print an integer list, JoinIntegers returns comma-separated values without a trailing delimiter.

guides.title: C# arrays, tuples, and nullable construction
guides.summary: Make shape, allocation, and ordering explicit.

sections.title: Jagged is not automatically rectangular
paragraphs: int[][] is an array of row references. Rows can be null or have different lengths. int[,] is a rectangular multidimensional array with two indices. Many coding platforms use jagged signatures, but inspect the supplied signature rather than assuming a universal platform rule.

Before reading grid[0].Length, handle an empty outer array. Before applying one column count to every row, rely on a stated rectangular contract or validate it. The reference grid methods validate shape; AllocateGrid creates one distinct row array for every row.

sections.title: Allocation and initialization
paragraphs: new int[n] is initialized to zeros; new bool[n] to false; a reference array starts with null entries. Array.Fill(array,-1) replaces every entry. For a jagged bool grid, allocate the outer array and then each row separately.

If you reuse the same row object for every slot, changing one apparent row changes them all. For rectangular storage, new int[m,n] allocates one multidimensional object. State both element count and representation when estimating space; an n×n int table uses roughly 4n² bytes for values alone.

sections.title: Tuples in queues, keys, and comparisons
paragraphs: Queue<(int Row,int Column)> can store coordinates without a custom class; deconstruct a removed value with var (r,c)=queue.Dequeue(). Named elements improve readability but are not separate runtime identity. Value tuples are value types and are useful dictionary keys when their component equality matches the state.

The default comparer for comparable tuple components orders lexicographically, so Array.Sort on (int,int) coordinates sorts row first, then column. C# does not provide tuple < or > syntax, and arbitrary component types may not be orderable. Equality support and ordering support are distinct.

sections.title: Create only when absent
paragraphs: The expression child ??= new Node() evaluates the right side only if child is null, then assigns it. It is convenient in trie insertion and lazy initialization. It does not make initialization thread-safe or validate an array index.

For a nullable child reference, once the operation completes normally the child is non-null. The complete Trie.cs implementation validates lowercase input first and shows the operation in a working data structure rather than an isolated placeholder.

guides.title: C# overflow, sentinels, and safe bounds
guides.summary: Choose the numeric type before arithmetic occurs.

sections.title: Widen an operand, not only the destination
paragraphs: Assigning a*b to a long does not fix an overflow that already happened in int arithmetic. Cast an operand first: (long)a*b. Similarly, (long)a+b widens the sum before evaluation. Summing 100,000 values near one billion needs about 10^14, comfortably beyond int.

Use checked when overflow should fail rather than wrap, and state the supported numeric range. long is larger, not infinite. For unbounded counts, BigInteger may be appropriate, with time and memory depending on bit length. The examples use long for sums and products under explicit input bounds.

sections.title: Infinity is a state, not a normal addend
paragraphs: int.MaxValue, int.MinValue, and long.MaxValue are finite extreme values. If long.MaxValue means “unreachable,” test for that state before adding an edge weight. Adding to a sentinel can overflow or produce a plausible but meaningless value.

A sentinel can collide with legitimate data. Nullable values, a Try method, or a separate boolean is often safer for “missing.” double.PositiveInfinity follows floating-point rules and should not be substituted into exact integer arithmetic without considering precision.

sections.title: Midpoint safety depends on the bounds
paragraphs: lo+(hi-lo)/2 avoids overflow from lo+hi when lo and hi are nonnegative int array indices and their difference fits int. Across the full signed int range, hi-lo can itself overflow. Numerics.Midpoint widens both the difference and addition to long before converting the in-range midpoint back to int.

For full-range long bounds, a further strategy is needed: narrower documented bounds, unsigned arithmetic with a proof, or BigInteger. Never label a formula universally overflow-safe without stating its domain. In answer-search examples here, nonnegative capacities fit long and their difference also fits.
sections.example: Midpoint(int.MinValue,int.MaxValue) is -1 with the widened calculation; doing hi-lo in int is unsafe.

guides.title: Memoization and recursion depth
guides.summary: Caching repeated states changes work, but does not remove the call stack.

sections.title: Cache by the complete logical state
paragraphs: Memoization stores the answer to a subproblem so later visits avoid recomputing it. In LCS, the pair (i,j) identifies remaining suffixes, so a Dictionary<(int,int),int> is a valid key. Query it after base cases; compute and store on a miss. Zero is a valid cached answer, so TryGetValue must decide presence.

A key must include every input that can change the answer. If a backtracking result depends on a visited set or remaining budget, caching only the current coordinate is wrong. Likewise, keep the memo local or clear it when the original input changes. Number of states times work per state is the useful complexity model: LCS has O(mn) states.

sections.title: Recursion can still be linear depth
paragraphs: A skewed tree, a long linked list, or a thin grid component can make recursion depth O(n). The safe depth depends on runtime stack size and frame size, so there is no universal safe cutoff such as 100,000. C# does not guarantee tail-call optimization for ordinary recursive methods.

Convert to an explicit stack or iterative DP when depth can be large. Preserve the work that recursion was doing: a postorder computation may need frames with an “expanded” flag or saved child results, while a simple reachability DFS needs only node identities. Memoization reduces repeated branches but may leave the longest chain unchanged.

guides.title: Read constraints as a budget, not a lookup table
guides.summary: Estimate actual work and memory, then choose the simplest feasible algorithm.

sections.title: n around 10–12: factorial output is already large
paragraphs: n! counts permutations, but “n<=12” does not guarantee a factorial algorithm is fast enough. 10! is 3,628,800; 12! is 479,001,600. Materializing every 12-element permutation requires billions of stored integers before object overhead. Even generating without storing has enormous output cost.

Use small-n constraints as permission to investigate exhaustive search, pruning, symmetry reduction, or dynamic programming over subsets. Estimate nodes visited and cost per leaf, not only the asymptotic label. If the prompt literally requires all permutations, explain that output size itself limits scaling.

sections.title: n around 20–25: subsets may be borderline
paragraphs: 2^20 is about one million and 2^25 about 33.6 million. A constant-time bit operation per subset differs radically from copying 25 items or scanning all pairs for every subset. O(n·2^n) and O(2^n) are not interchangeable budgets.

Bitmask DP can fit some small-n optimization tasks, but it is an advanced follow-on here. First learn ordinary backtracking and one-dimensional DP. Count states, transitions, memory per state, and output volume before deciding enumeration is acceptable.

sections.title: n around 100: cubic can be plausible; quartic is costly
paragraphs: 100^3 is one million inner operations, while 100^4 is one hundred million. These are different practical workloads even before allocation, hashing, or complex transitions. A “2-D DP” label does not imply O(n³) or O(n⁴): dimensions and transition work determine time.

Floyd-Warshall is O(V³) for all-pairs paths, interval DP is often O(n³), and simple two-string DP is O(mn). Identify the actual loops. Do not memorize a range as a promise that every algorithm within it meets an unspecified time limit.

sections.title: n around 500: verify cubic cost carefully
paragraphs: 500³ is 125 million iterations. That may be too slow for a heavy C# transition or tight interview platform budget. A 500×500 int table has roughly one million bytes of element payload, but additional object structures can cost much more.

Compare the known O(n³) approach to possible O(n²) or O(n² log n) alternatives, but avoid inventing an optimization you cannot justify. State estimated work and ask about time/memory limits if they are absent.

sections.title: n around 5,000: quadratic is 25 million
paragraphs: A simple O(n²) loop at 5,000 elements does around 25 million iterations (or half that for unordered pairs). A 5,000² int table is about 100 MB of payload, which may exceed memory limits even when the running time is acceptable.

A streaming pair comparison and a full pair table have the same time order but different memory requirements. Rolling rows, two-pointer elimination, or hashing may help when their invariants match the problem. Treat both time and space as first-class constraints.

sections.title: n around 100,000: sorting is a useful baseline
paragraphs: n log2 n is about 1.7 million at n=100,000, while n² is ten billion. This often rules out all pairs and makes sorting, heaps, or balanced trees attractive. The exact constant factors and the cost of comparison still matter.

Hash-based O(n) expected-time algorithms can beat sorting, but sorting may be deterministic, compact, and simpler. Choose the cleanest approach satisfying the budget, and distinguish expected, amortized, and worst-case complexity.

sections.title: Millions of elements: scans and memory traffic matter
paragraphs: At n=10^6 to 10^7, a few linear passes may be appropriate, while per-element allocation, large maps, and input parsing can dominate. An int array of ten million elements alone contains about 40 MB of payload. O(n) memory may still be too much.

Sliding windows, prefix sums, and hashing are possible linear techniques, but each has a contract and memory tradeoff. A linear algorithm can perform many expensive operations per item; Big-O does not measure wall-clock time directly.

sections.title: A huge numeric range is not necessarily huge input
paragraphs: A numeric bound such as 10^18 may describe an answer range, not a count of stored elements. Binary searching that integer range needs roughly 60 predicate checks, but each check might scan an input of size n, for total O(n log range).

If n really is the length of an explicitly supplied unsorted array, reading it alone costs Ω(n); you cannot usually solve an arbitrary property in O(log n). Large value ranges suggest arithmetic or answer search only when the problem structure supports them.

guides.title: A repeatable coding interview workflow
guides.summary: Make your reasoning inspectable and your assumptions testable.

sections.title: Think aloud at useful decision points
paragraphs: Explain the goal, the current hypothesis, and why you are testing it. If stuck, say what is failing: “The nested loop is correct but quadratic; I’m looking for a way to reuse work between adjacent windows.” That gives the interviewer something concrete to respond to.

There is no universal 20-second silence rule, and interviewers differ in how they give hints. Short quiet thinking is normal. Avoid narrating every keystroke; instead signal assumptions, invariants, changes of approach, and test results. If you need a moment, say so briefly.

sections.title: Clarify, baseline, improve, implement, test
paragraphs: Restate the input/output contract: duplicates, empty input, index base, mutation permission, ordering, and numeric bounds. Give a correct baseline before optimizing. Explain the key invariant and target time/space, then check for questions if the interviewer is engaging. You do not need a ritual permission request before every implementation.

After coding, trace a small normal example and purposeful edge cases: empty/singleton, duplicates, missing target, extreme values, disconnected graph, or invalid shape as relevant. Explain any validation you omit because constraints guarantee it. Keep an unaided first attempt before opening this guide; afterward record the actual gap (recognition, derivation, C# syntax, correctness, or speed), not just whether the final code looks familiar.

Interview formats vary by company and round, including whether AI tools are permitted. Verify the current instructions for the specific role rather than assuming a universal environment. This curriculum supports reasoning and implementation you can perform independently; it is not a guarantee of every possible interview topic.
sections.example: A concise plan: “I’ll keep prior values in a map so each number needs one complement lookup. That is expected O(n) time and O(n) memory. I’ll test duplicate values and no match.”

guides.title: Graph modeling before traversal
guides.summary: Define vertices, edges, direction, and visited state before choosing BFS or DFS.

sections.title: Adjacency lists and disconnected components
paragraphs: An adjacency list stores each vertex’s outgoing neighbors. For an undirected edge add both directions; for a directed edge add only the stated direction. Explicitly create all vertices, including isolated ones. For a graph with V vertices and E edges, lists typically use O(V+E) storage, while an adjacency matrix uses O(V²).

A traversal from one start reaches only its component. To cover the whole graph, loop over every vertex and start a new traversal for each unseen one. Mark on scheduling so cycles cannot keep adding work. Graphs.Components supplies an iterative undirected example, including isolated nodes and an empty graph.

The state may be richer than the visible node: a puzzle can use board configurations as vertices, while a constrained route can use (location,remainingBudget). A visited set keyed too coarsely can incorrectly prune a solution. Conversely, a tree normally needs no visited set if the input is truly acyclic and child pointers never lead upward.

Before coding, state whether self-loops or repeated edges are allowed, whether the graph is directed, and whether you need reachability, a shortest path, a dependency order, or connectivity under updates. These are different outputs even when the same adjacency list can represent them.
